utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May I have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, all. For the Prosecution, I'm Tom Hannis along with Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic, appearing for the Stanisic Defence this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic for the Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Macar. Before I invite Mr. Zecevic to continue, I remind you, you're still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Macar.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, yesterday, toward the end, we discussed document 1D94, which is at tab 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I kindly ask for that document to be displayed again. Could the usher please hand this binder to the witness. [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 46. You told us that this document was signed by Mr. Vujicic, the chief analyst of the RS MUP.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the last-but-one paragraph, there's an instruction that the Sarajevo CSB compiled a detailed report on the measures to prevent crime with statistic indicators, according to criminal offences reported and discovered, et cetera. Do you remember if the CSB ever did that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The Sarajevo CSB did actually compile such a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us show the witness 1D188, please. That's at tab 47.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We saw that the previous document was dated 23 August. There is no date on this document. But, on page 2, there's a reference to a letter from the Ministry of Justice which was received on the 25th of August. We can read that in the last paragraph. Is this that report of the CSB mentioned in that letter?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is the very report, and I believe that there was also a cover letter. But this is the report. Reference is made here to the document from the Ministry of Justice and the document that we have just seen in the paragraph you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, yesterday we spoke about that letter from the prime minister and the other letter from the Ministry of Justice, and on page 22930 of yesterday's transcript, you mentioned a campaign against the Ministry of the Interior, including the minister personally, Minister Stanisic. Apart from the prime minister and his deputy, as well as some members of parliament were involved, and so was Ms. Plavsic, as a member of the Presidency. Before that, you had said that there had been a clash between Mr. Stanisic and Djeric regarding that campaign. What was the basic objection of Prime Minister Djeric and these other persons to the work of the ministry and the minister personally?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me first point out the following: I was able to contact the then-Prime Minister Djeric, whom I know personally. He wasn't a man all too familiar with the functioning of public administration. The minister of the interior of Republika Srpska, Mr. Stanisic, without the assistance of the cabinet or other line ministries, could not create on his own the necessary preconditions for the normal functioning of the MUP. It is understandable that requests, especially from the administrations at headquarters, where certain weaknesses were identified whilst touring on the ground, were conveyed to the minister, and he in turn conveyed them to the Prime Minister, asking that the cabinet implement certain measures faster. We realised that other ministries were also created from scratch, but Mr. Stanisic, just as he expected us to do some things faster, also tried to get it done through the cabinet. But the problems in Vogosca, especially with regard to TAS, were used to blame the Ministry of the Interior. The ministry was blamed for the situation in Vogosca, and not only Vogosca, also Rajlovac and Ilidza, maybe. In Vogosca, there were large stocks of goods, not only at TAS but in other factories, too. And then the ministry initiated the relocation of vehicles to prevent pillage and destruction due to combat operations, but there was strong resistance from the municipal authorities, that is, the Crisis Staff, and information started going laterally toward the cabinet and Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, sir, but I must, again, ask you to speak slowly. Part of your answer wasn't recorded. It was recorded that the minister was blamed for this situation in Vogosca. I believe that you said something else.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not the minister. There was an attempt --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP, not the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So it was the ministry?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the ministry as an administrative body.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please continue and explain slowly.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the unsuccessful proposal to relocate to a territory which was not susceptible to combat operations and which can be physically secured, the vehicles remained in the Vogosca municipality in the same space which could be exposed to combat operations and under the control of the Vogosca Crisis Staff. And something similar happened in Rajlovac where there were large stocks of goods, including oil and various consumables. And it was similar in Ilidza. The Crisis Staffs wanted to be in control of that property. That was one side of the story. And the minister requested the government that the judicial bodies be finally set up, that is, courts and public prosecutor's offices, without which the police couldn't function. But the preparations, especially in the prosecutor's office, were very slow, and the process of nominating new prosecutors took a long time. And there was lateral information flow, that is not vertical or official, in other words, to blame the ministry for general crime, whereas, the non-existence of judicial bodies was neglected. Behind these initiatives, there were some individuals who tried to conceal their own inactivity, and it was, in fact, the Crisis Staff who wanted to be in control of those goods to be able to distribute them as they thought fit; and, on the other hand, it was our intention to place all these under the control of the commodity reserves of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us sum this up, sir. In your opinion, was the position of the minister and the ministry in line with the laws and regulations that were in force?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Because, under the law, all stocks of goods, unprotected goods, were to be placed under the control of the commodity reserves authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And if I understood you correctly, some individuals from Crisis Staffs and local authorities who had effective control over these goods in their territory didn't like that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. The Crisis Staffs didn't like that because we had already observed that some of these goods were being sold, allegedly in order to buy either food for the citizens, or uniforms, or whatever, which was certainly beyond the control of the RS. And it -- approval for every such transaction was required; approval either from the government or from the commodity reserves authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us look at P427.8, which is tab 44.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a report on some aspects of the work done to date and the tasks ahead. This document was compiled by the MUP and distributed, as we can see, to the president of the Presidency and the prime minister. It was made after the first collegium of the ministry which took place on 11 July 1992. Were you familiar with this document in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All these problems we discussed on Tuesday, all these problems that the ministry faced. And we listed them and you commented. Are all these problems listed in this document which was submitted to the president of the Presidency and the prime minister?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that nearly all problems of which the MUP headquarters was aware are listed in this report and submitted to the authorities in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us just comment on what is written on page 4. And that's page 5 in e-court. It may be page 4 in English. I'm afraid that we'll have to move to the following page in English. Or, actually, no. We should have gone back to page 3; I apologise. Page 3 in English. It's because the line spacing of the original is greater. In English, the -- it's the fourth paragraph from the bottom; and in the original, it's the second paragraph from the top. And it's about war crimes. It was pointed out that the priority for both the national service and the crime investigation service is to detect war crimes, provide documentation (then which documentation) and file criminal reports. Documents also provided for war crimes committed by Serbs. Tell me, sir, does this faithfully reflect the position of the ministry at that period?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This probably faithfully reflects the position of the ministry and the minister, as well as the collegium and the crime police administration and directorate at the HQ. I'd just like to point out one thing: In addition to what the report says, at all the meetings and briefings that we had with the minister, there was one general position. Crimes were never broken down the ethnic lines. The general attitude was always that we were trying to shed light on war crimes, and that certainly was very much the position taken by the HQ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Macar, I think I understand what your -- what you last said as probably being a partial answer to the question I'm about to ask, but the -- whereas, on the one hand, the document says what it says, there is -- and it may be a fault of the interpretation, but your answer was, "This probably reflects the position of the ministry," and I'm wondering why you use the word "probably." As I said, I'm not unmindful of the remainder of your answer, but could you explain why you said -- why you used the word "probably"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That might be somewhat inaccurate. I did say probably but this is, generally speaking, the position of the Ministry of the Interior, to shed light on war crimes regardless of the ethnic background of the citizens and persons involved. If I said probably, this is because this is just an extract. There are more documents previously produced about this by the minister, the chief of the crime police, documents that provided a more comprehensive overview of war crimes and the position taken in that respect. The general position taken by everyone there was that we needed to work, in order to shed light on war crimes, regardless of the victims' ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let us try and clarify this. I think you said "for the most part" and not "probably." Let me make sure I understand what you're trying to say. Is it your position that this document does not contain all of the problems that the ministry was encountering in its work? Is that what you were trying to say?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what I was trying to say. There was some previous documents that we analysed and used where we offered a far broader view of these problems, all of the problems that we were encountering, and that also included specific guide-lines for the work of the SJBs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If there is any need, we can go through the document in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, could you remind me the tab number of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The document tab number 34. It's P427.8. 34. [Interpretation] Could we please look at page 3 of the Serbian, which I assume to be page 2 in the English. Actually not. It's the page that's already on the screen. So the English is good. Paragraph 2 states: "The shortage of personnel in all MUP services is also a limiting factor. Many documents are missing. There are no penal records, registers," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was that another problem that you encountered?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Next paragraph: "The political situation is greatly affecting the rifts." I'll skip a portion there: "In other communities, local politics is exerting a powerful influence." Was this a problem too?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a large-scale problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Next paragraph: "In some communities, neither the military nor the civilian judiciary is functioning. Judges have not been elected. And in Bosanska Krajina, for instance, several thousand court cases have not yet been resolved. There are no judges for criminal cases. Judges receive threats and are in fear. The courts do not function and hardened criminals are released from prison, which affects the establishment of the rule of law and the work of law enforcement organs." Was this, too, one of the problems that you discussed and testified about over the last couple of days?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I did say that in the previous part of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Next page, the last paragraph on page 4 of the Serbian reads -- which is the second-to-last paragraph in the English: "A new political and territorial division of the RS was being prepared which will replace the previously necessary forms such as autonomous Serb areas and regions with districts." Are you familiar with this, sir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let us go to page 6, paragraph 2, which is the next page in the English. It reads: "What is not negotiable is the fact that the Ministry of the Interior ..." It's the third paragraph from the bottom of the page up in the English: "What is not negotiable is the fact that the Ministry of the Interior is a professional organisation, not influenced by politics. This means not influenced by individuals, groups, factions and parties." Do you remember this being the position of the highest ranking employees of the Ministry of the Interior at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In most municipalities and SJBs, we would come across local politicians exercising a great degree of influence, and also the Crisis Staffs, too. It was the position of the ministry, right from the outset, that the Ministry of the Interior should provide approval and formalise appointments in SJBs and CSBs in keeping with the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Zecevic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Page 9, the last paragraph, talks about the prevention and documenting of war crimes. That's page 10 in the Serbian, in e-court, and I assume page 8 of the English. It's probably page 7. Or 6. Yes. Paragraph 3 of page 6. It reads: "Preventing and documenting war crimes by using all legally prescribed methods for documenting such activities ..." Do you remember that this, too, was emphasised by the ministry at the time and that was also its position?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The administration was involved in formalising this request on working methods. And we inserted deliberately what can you see in the brackets here: Photographs, audio recordings, expert opinions, medical findings, witness and eye-witness testimony. As I said earlier in my evidence, the Ministry of the Interior was under-equipped, in terms of materiel and technology, and this applied to our public security stations as well the CSBs. We were unable to create the logistical conditions quickly enough to equip those stations, particularly when it came to photograph and film equipment and technology. Based on the pre-war organisation of the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were labs, photo labs, in CSBs so that it would sometimes be the case that certain rolls of film would just lie there for weeks on end without being developed; whereas, there were some private labs which ended up developing those rolls.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, page 11 in e-court, page 10 for you, the English reference is the page that we have. That's two paragraphs down. It reads: "To resolve these problems and the dispute over jurisdiction between the MUP and the Army of the Serbian Republic ..." The next paragraph talks about resolving existing problems and outstanding issues with the justice ministry. Do you remember whether these problems were discussed at any of the collegium meetings of the Ministry of the Interior of the RS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Zecevic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Along the same lines, on the next page, it's still the present page in the English. It reads, in paragraph 1: "In keeping with the Law on Criminal Procedure and the Law on Internal Affairs, and in order for the MUP to only process persons before the actual trial or before their hand-over to the judicial organs, which is the result of the work of the SUP [as interpreted], there needs to be ..." The second-to-last paragraph in the English: "Special emphasis should be placed on the issue of relocating certain citizens, villages, et cetera, because this does not fall within the competence of the MUP, although efforts are being made to link it to the MUP." Do you remember whether this subject, too, is something that was discussed at the collegium meetings of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What we see here, is it consistent with the position that you took at the collegium meetings?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Last paragraph, last sentence in the English. The next paragraph of the Serbian and the last sentence in the English: "Another conclusion was that the MUP must be funded solely from the budget of the Serbian Republic ..." Was that another position taken at one of those meetings of the ministry at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the position of the Ministry of the Interior of the RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, this note or information was submitted to the highest ranking bodies of the RS at the time: The president of the Presidency, and the prime minister. You submitted all these requests and all this information. Did those bodies do anything about it; and, if so, what?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I personally observed and what I remember is that after this information was made available and after the meetings of the minister with the president and prime minister, the pace increased, the pace of establishing judicial organs, both civilian ones and in the military. I also think that the commodity reserve administration's work improved. If I may add, concerning the last conclusion that you read, which deals with the confiscated items, perhaps the formulation here was a bit clumsy, as I know that it was a suggestion coming from the crime police and crime police administration; namely, that the confiscated items that some citizens took from abandoned houses and so on, and we learned about it when they crossed check-points and so on, that all of these confiscated items should be put under the jurisdiction of the commodity reserves administration. We didn't know where these items came from, and the commodity reserves administration had its municipal commissions who could take in the confiscated items. Overall, the pressure on the ministry still existed. The ministry had its planned activities. And owing to that, its work, the organisation of its work, continually improved. However, due to objections and complaints concerning judicial organ, complaints which said that the ministry did not work well, the pressure of even greater intensity continued. And this pressure came from one part of the government cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me show you several orders of the Ministry of the Interior so that we can illustrate the point; namely, what the ministry did following the circulation of this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 1D58, tab 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, this order is dated 23rd of July, 1992, signed by Minister Mico Stanisic. In the preamble, it say: "Proceeding from the conclusions reached at the meeting of executive employees held on 11 July 1992, the meeting of the collegium ... on 23rd July, 1992, at the minister's enactment," number such and such, "this order is being adopted, or issued." Tell me, do you know about this order?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what was the reason behind this order, if you know? Why was it issued?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation with the war territory of Republika Srpska and Bosnia and Herzegovina, and especially the large number of refugees who had come from the territory under the control of Croatian and Muslim forces, as well as an increase in the number of crimes committed, all made it necessary to increase the number of active and reserve policemen in the municipal organs of the interior and SJBs, as well as staff members of the crime police. The Ministry of the Interior, in its headquarters, received information that in certain SJBs and in the municipal organs of the interior, certain persons joined the reserve force who previously had been convicted, who had a criminal record. A particular problem, as we could see in the previous document that we saw, the previous information, was that, due to war operations, certain records were destroyed, and I will tell you exactly which regards later on. Also, there was a large influx of residents coming from the territory under the control of Muslim and Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, I apologise. I have to interrupt you. Our time is limited. We have a lot of documents, and I would like us to focus on the questions. My question was: What was the reason for issuing this order, such an order? If you can give us a one-sentence answer.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason for issuing this order was that they realised that reserve police forces had among its members people who had criminal records, who had convictions, criminal convictions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The fact that somebody was convicted for crimes committed, did that affect that person's ability to become a member of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: People with criminal convictions were not eligible to become members of the Ministry of the Interior in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 1D59, which is a document of the Ministry of the Interior, sent to CSBs, dated the 24th of July, dealing with the same issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you can tell us who signed it. It says here "for the minister of the interior," and we see somebody's signature.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my signature. And this was done pursuant to the request of Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, we see that in this document they give an instruction that members of the ministry who had been criminally prosecuted or against whom there were proceedings pending, ought to be dismissed from their service in the ministry. Tell me, please, based on this document, they were supposed to be dismissed from which position, from which service?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were supposed to be dismissed from their jobs in the Ministry of the Interior, both in active or reserve force, although we did not have information that there were any such persons within the active police force, persons with criminal convictions. They were mostly in reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The fact that these persons were being relieved of their duties in the ministry and that they were being placed at the disposal of the army, did it in any way affect any pending criminal proceedings against these individuals?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it says here in the document, all of those who had criminal convictions, meaning that they had already been convicted by any court in Bosnia and Herzegovina for crimes committed, the criminal records in Bosnia and Herzegovina were kept in the jurisdiction where they resided. And we needed access to those records to know whether somebody had criminal convictions. Due to the fact that there was a lot of movement of the population --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you. I apologise. We are clear on that. So if somebody had a criminal conviction, then that person wasn't eligible to become a member of the ministry. Then -- you have already explained that to us. My question was this: What about proceedings, criminal proceedings, that were under way, that were ongoing at that particular moment against certain individuals who were then relieved of their duties in the ministry and placed at the disposal of the army? Did this document that we now see affect in any way the criminal responsibility and any pending criminal proceedings against those persons at that moment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Criminal proceedings take some time, and in cases where we learned that there were any pending criminal proceedings in the territory of Republika Srpska, such persons could not become members of the Ministry of the Interior, and they were placed at the disposal of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you yet again. Were criminal proceedings against these persons terminated due to the fact that they were relieved of their duties in the Ministry of the Interior and placed at the disposal of the Army of Republika Srpska? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because criminal proceedings fall under the jurisdiction of judicial organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I see the time. Are we implementing the same schedule today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I assumed that that schedule would run for the duration of this witness's testimony. So we take a break and resume in 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, I'm going to show you document 1D176, which is at tab 41. Before commenting on this document, let me ask you something. Maybe you can give us a brief explanation. Here's a hypothetical example for you to explain how things were dealt with at the time. If the MUP were to hire a person who was a former employee of the MUP in a place which was outside the Serbian territory -- Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, let's say Tuzla as an example, were you, at the ministry, able to come by the personal file of that person?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to come by any police file of that person, if his or her residence was previously outside the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How did you get information that the person in question may have been -- may have stood trial for a criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received such information from individual refugees from those areas, or possibly from some former MUP members who had left those areas and were hired by our MUP. In such cases, since we were unable to get more in-depth information of that nature, such persons were returned to the VRS, to be at their disposal, and that went through the Ministry of National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This order dated 27 July 1992 comprises a total of 11 items. Are you familiar with this order, which is signed by the minister, Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In item 2 of this order, for the second or third time, reference is made to that order of 23 July that we saw, with regard to the differentiation between -- or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: In the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is to say the removal of persons who were not eligible to be ministry employees. In item 4, we read that all special units established during the war in the areas of Security Services Centres, must be disbanded immediately and placed under the command of the Army of the Serbian Republic. It goes on to discuss the special purposes police detachment of the MUP of the RS. If you know, tell us what the reason was for disbanding these special units and what the reason was for the establishment of the special purposes police units in the areas of the CSBs.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The disbanding of special units that had been established in the framework of CSBs was done because the ministry never approved their establishment. Their members had not been vetted. And they didn't have decisions on appointment from the ministry headquarters. At that time, there was this strong inclination to use police for combat operations, and many such units were resubordinated to the VRS and basically spent their time at the front line. The complex security situation in the RS required a much higher level of organisation of special units which were to be used primarily for security purposes, and only secondarily for defence. That's why it was decided that a police detachment be established which was under the direct command of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That police detachment which was under the direct command of the MUP, who was its immediate commander?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milenko Karisik was its direct commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After this order, that is, in the second half of 1992, did this unit have platoons with all CSBs in the territory of the Serbian Republic of BH?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the setting up of police detachments, organisational units were established with the CSBs. They were not commanded by the CSBs but they shared their facilities. But they were still under the direct command of Mr. Karisik; that is, of the MUP. And the decision to relocate parts of the unit to the centres was due to the fragmentation of the territory and the complex security situation which required efficient responses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show the witness 678D1, which is at tab 42.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a document dated 30 July 1992. The author of the document is the War Presidency of Trebinje municipality. Its president, Bozidar Vucurevic, is ordering that the special police platoon of the Trebinje CSB be disbanded. The fact that the president of the War Presidency issued an order to disband a special police platoon is something that we would like to hear your comment on. What happened here?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already stated which problems the MUP faced with regard to the leaders of the Crisis Staffs or the autonomous regions. There were attempts on their part to control the security organs in their territory. It is unusual for Mr. Vucurevic to issue such an order and he sent it to the Trebinje CSB, and this exercise on the part of the -- of Mr. Vucurevic was not in line with the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please wait a moment, please. Not -- your entire reply was not recorded. The previous order that we have seen signed by Minister Stanisic, who was to implement the order to disband these units?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chiefs of the CSBs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Who was chief of the Trebinje CSB; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, it was Krsto Savic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, instead of a decision of the chief of the CSB, Mr. Savic, there's an order by the president of the War Presidency. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is obvious that Mr. Savic also had problems in the territory of the Trebinje centre because some individuals thought that their role was much stronger than what was envisaged by the law, and this is an example of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document into evidence, unless there are objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D642, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P605, tab 58, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a document of the Banja Luka CSB, dated 19 August, signed by the chief of the centre, Stojan Zupljanin, and it was distributed to all SJBs in their territory. It says re: Order of the minister of the interior of 10 August 1992 and the dispatch of 17 August 1992. And the contents of these are related in its entirety. Items 1 and 2 spell out detention measures and security of the collection centres. Are you familiar with this order of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Through the police administration, and 03 is their classification mark. And through the analytics department, whose classification mark is 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Under the law, how long could the police detain a person suspected of committing a crime?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the Law on Criminal Procedure, up to three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 1 says that measures of detention and custody can only be applied within the existing rules. What is that in relation to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Custody and detention could only be imposed within the premises of the SJBs and CSBs; for example, while a person was being interviewed. As for detention, that also applied to the justice system, including the prisons that were under the justice ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Where it says here existing rules or regulations, what is that in reference to? Is that in reference to the provisions of the Law on Criminal Procedure that we commented on a while ago?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Law on Criminal Procedure of the RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you see this after item 2, it talks about the -- securing the collection centres that's -- are under the VRS. It says that disciplinary measures, and, if necessary, other measures shall be taken against those not in compliance. And it goes on, the last portion of the paragraph: "For the implementation of this order, I will take measures as prescribed by the law against any commanders in the organisational unit which is their responsibility under Zupljanin." In the last paragraph, again, says: "I once again repeat that the order should be made urgently and in a consistent manner. Please immediately inform the Banja Luka CSB about the result ..." Sir, can you please explain why many of these orders that we have been looking at seem to stress the responsibility of employees in the leading positions in the Ministry of the Interior, and that all these constant threats being made of disciplinary and other measures that might be taken against them, in keeping with the existing laws. Why is that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, the interior minister, Mr. Stanisic, was very consistent in his application of the law. Whenever there was a meeting with the heads of public and state security units and other leaders, he was adamant every time that one had to work in compliance with the Law on Criminal procedure and all the other laws that were security related and affected the security situation. The same information was passed along down the chain of command to those working in the field, in order to step up discipline in those segments that the ministry could directly affect and in reference to those appointments that the ministry itself had made. In some of the SJBs, we couldn't have a proper subordination system of those because all of the people in the leading positions there had been appointed by the local Crisis Staffs and the municipal bodies, so the Ministry of the Interior and the centre did not have an appropriate role to play, such as that envisaged by the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D48, tab 94. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a dispatch from very late in 1992. The date is the 17th of December, 1992. Addressed to all CSBs chiefs, all the directorates at the HQ, and all the public security stations. Signed by Minister Mico Stanisic. Conclusion was adopted that it is necessary to conduct checks of all MUP employees through operative, misdemeanour and criminal records. Again, it says: "All persons with a criminal record and employees with a negative operative checks are to be relieved of duty immediately in accordance with the Law on Internal Affairs. "Deadline: 15 days. "Failure to carry out this task in the set period will be punished most severely. "I forbid the payment of wages to employees who have not been checked." Are you familiar with this ministry dispatch, sir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please comment on the dispatch? Explain what it is in reference to.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the end of 1992, the Ministry of the Interior had created conditions and rules to have personal files on each and every employee of the Ministry of the Interior. This, above all, implied that the numbers of both the active and reserve forces should be organised in keeping with the assessments of the actual situation on the ground in the various municipalities. It was sometimes the case in certain public security stations that this order was not complied with, or at least not fully, in terms of increasing or reducing the number of reservists, which was very much a function of the security situation that prevailed in a certain area. On the other hand, based on the existing documentation and the records throughout the RS, our intention was to keep the files as up to date as possible on all of our workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I see an order here by Mr. Stanisic, the then-minister, forbidding the payment of wages, of salaries. This being December 1992, up until December 1992, was the ministry already being financed from the federal budget, and was there a centralised payment system through the Ministry of the Interior, through which all members of the ministry throughout the territory received their salaries?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that applied to most of the territory. But there were certain public security stations that failed to obey the order in establishing this centralised system through which salaries were then paid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D522, tab 88.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this document was signed by Minister Mico Stanisic. It's another dispatch from late in 1992. The number is 10-013, and it is addressed to the municipal assemblies, the president, and the chairman of the Executive Board. It's about persons being proposed for leading positions in the ministry. Paragraph 2 reads: "We wish to inform you that, given the emphasised legal responsibility of the chief of the Security Services Centre for the general security situation in the area of the centre, the ministry has set relevant norms, according to which chiefs of these centres are the only ones authorised to recommend ... personnel ... for appointment in their respective areas, including the SJBs." Sir, are you familiar with this dispatch?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with the dispatch, and it is a result of feedback received following the minister's order relating to the method of personnel verification in the CSBs and SJBs. There were certain anomalies in some municipalities where the heads of CSBs were not able to have normal communication with the municipal leaders and appoint proposed candidates to certain positions due to obstruction by municipal leadership. And that is why the minister, after some meetings, had no choice but to send this and remind municipal leaders of responsibilities of the Ministry of the Interior under the law and the procedures of the Ministry of the Interior concerning the selection of personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This dispatch that serves to remind the municipal presidents and presidents of Executive Boards, how successful was it? Did it yield any particular results; and, if so, what kind? Partial results, full results?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some municipalities –- in some municipalities, even despite this –- instruction, not to say a warning, there were no results whatsoever, and perhaps even more obstruction ensued.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, let me ask you this: What is the basic function of the crime administration of the MUP attached to the headquarters, in relation to the CSBs across the territory?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the functions would include monitoring the work of the crime squads across the stations, providing technical assistance, proposing measures and activities to combat any emerging forms of crime. Generally speaking, training employees by organising courses and seminars, collecting information regarding the situation across the police stations and forwarding this to the centre, particularly the relevance service in charge of materiel and technical assistance. Personnel assessments and such-like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did the crime administration of the Ministry of the Interior attached to the HQ, which is where you first worked as a co-ordinator, and then you held a leading position, that of one of the heads, did the administration tour these CSBs and inspect these CSBs throughout the RS; and, if so, when -- from when on?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, we didn't have formal inspections. We did tour these institutions, and we performed some training in both the CSBs and the SJBs further afield. I think the first visit included meeting the heads at the Sarajevo CSB, and then towards the end of the year, we started taking up activities with the other centres, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the month this occurred, the first instructive tour or visit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first meeting with the heads of the crime squads in the Sarajevo CSB I believe occurred in February. I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreter is not sure about the month the witness mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It says February. Which month did you mention?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: July 1992. But I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At the very outset, I asked you a question, and you said that back in 1992 you did not do formal inspection, formal monitoring. What was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to perform a formal audit of one of the stations or centres, or the centre itself, first of all, some time is required, and you need to enlist the assistance of quite a number of inspectors to be involved in that. You need to collect operative information from all of the police stations. No such audit could be performed competently unless, of course, you had between 10 and 15 days to spare in each of the stations. There were also these tours, as we called them. We would send out a number of inspectors and determine the exact number of days based on the existing resource, such as fuel, food. At one point, the number of days was determined based on the number of cans of canned food that we had to feed those inspectors working in the field. It was impossible to even get them a decent place to sleep in some of these places. We simply didn't have the kind of logistics that this required, and we had to make do. We used personal contacts. They would call on their friends. Sometimes there were hotels or restaurants operating in these areas and whatnot.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You explained about the Sarajevo Romanija-Birac CSB. You say that, as far as you remember, it happened in July 1992. Do you remember when the instructive tours of other CSBs occurred, such as those in Doboj, Banja Luka, and so on?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first inspection of the Doboj centre was conducted by the mixed team with members from two administrations. I think it was pursuant to a request of Mr. Kovac, who, at the time, was acting head of the public security department. As for the Banja Luka centre, it -- an inspection was planned for November. And prior to that, whether it was late August or early September, part of the Trebinje centre was also inspected, as well as Visegrad, Rudo, Cajnice and Foca. The Trebinje centre at the time could not conduct even basic functioning. They had no communications centre. And to reach them, one had to go via Montenegro. And we would go to Visegrad from Bijeljina, also via Serbia and Montenegro. I think that all of this is mentioned in the report that was drawn after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, please remind us, I think that you said it, but if you can tell us again, when did the crime prevention administration get transferred to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision to transfer the headquarters of the ministry to Bijeljina was issued in the second half of September. And then in early October, I personally took part in setting up the administration within the headquarters of the ministry, setting up the basic lines of work that needed to be operational, and so on. We had really only very few staff members. We were staffed at a very low level and couldn't even carry the basic functions with that amount of staff members. So the work was -- started in early October, and it continued through November.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, based on your recollection, why was this administration, as well as some other administrations and the headquarters, moved to Bijeljina in the second half of 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of its location. It was equidistant to Banja Luka and to Sarajevo. And also Bijeljina had many more resources needed for the headquarters than Pale. Pale is a small place, and it had very limited resources. And a large police facility, that was built before the war broke out, existed there. It had all the features needed to move the headquarters of the ministry to that place, and then it was possible to create the communication systems and everything else needed for the proper functioning of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, these -- these formal inspections, formal audits of the CSBs and SJBs were conducted by whom? Who was sent to conduct audits?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: A part of the activities was conducted pursuant to the head of the public security department. And, at that time, it was a mixed composition, with members from crime police and some other administrations within the ministry. And later on, it was the workers of the crime police administration who had been sent by the headquarters to perform that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally take part in any of these formal inspections, formal audits in the second half of 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally toured Doboj. I attended the meeting in Doboj. And inspectors, within their lines of work, inspected SJBs. My intention was, after Doboj, to tour the Banja Luka CSB and the Prijedor SJB because that was the plan. The security situation in Prijedor was out of our control, and the SJB was also outside of our control. It was clear that the CSB in Banja Luka could not control the work of the Prijedor SJB.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when Doboj, Prijedor, and Banja Luka were toured?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Doboj was toured in early November. I remember that it was extremely cold, minus 17 or 18. I think that we spent three days there. And what I particularly remember is that we slept in a -- in a demolished abandoned building. I think that it was the pensioners' centre. And there were no windows, no heating, but we had to sleep there in that cold. And then in November, at around the time of my birthday, which is the 14th of November, we went onto Banja Luka. And then we were supposed to go to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I'm a little bit confused here. A little while ago, the witness said that these inspections were no formal inspections nor audits. And then now you ask about, "Do you remember when Doboj, Prijedor, and Banja Luka" -- oh no, here you say "were toured." Did you personally take part in any of these formal inspections, formal audits? Are we talking about the formal ones or are we talking about the -- the witness answered "tours." Are we within the concept of we didn't do formal audits?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is, I guess, the interpretation. Because, Your Honour, there are two different -- two different terms and different procedures. One is -- I will say in Serbian. [Interpretation] Instructive audit is the first one; and instructive touring is the second one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would ask the witness to explain what is what.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in my question, I asked about the instructive touring or instructive visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead, Mr. Macar.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The terminology that we used was such that there was a visit, or touring, of the SJBs. The objective of which was to inform the organisational structure in the SJB within the crime service or elsewhere, to inform ourselves about the personnel matters, organisational matters that existed there in that SJB, as well as to see what equipment and materiel they had, as well as to learn about the crime rate and types of crimes in that area. When we say instructive visit or instructive touring, we refer to the visits made to SJBs in order to assist them, to give them advice about how crime service should operate or what action needs to be taken in a particular case. As for the instructive audit, or instructive supervision, that refers to the checks or inspection, as His Honour mentioned, of the work of the crime service, of each employee in the crime service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's a kind inspection that takes 15 days to -- to do; is that right? More or less.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At least 10 to 15 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And then you said, Mr. Macar: "I personally toured Doboj. I attended the meeting in Doboj. And inspectors, within their lines of work, inspected SJBs." Do you recall the names of those inspectors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not an inspection. It was a visit. Touring of the SJB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Touring, yes. Do you recall the names of the inspectors that toured those SJBs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, Sinisa Karan, Nikola Milanovic. Now whether Mitar Lukic from the white-collar crime section came, or one of his inspectors -- but I think it was Mitar Lukic. And then there was another member whose name just now escapes me. Perhaps it will come to me later in the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may add, I remember that there were five of us because we just barely fit into one car.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I see the time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we take the break now and resume in 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, let us just try to make things fully clear. Your trip to Doboj, Banja Luka, and Prijedor was that an instructive visit or something else?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a visit. That was our first opportunity to go to that area and learn about the situation that prevailed in the crime enforcement services, to get information about the security situation, and the functioning of the services in Prijedor, especially as there was information that the station there was not fully controlled by the CSB of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Macar, when was the first instructive audit conducted at the Banja Luka CSB and the SJBs that belonged to that centre, including the one in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: A partial instructive audit took place in September 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us return to November 1992. Was that visit to the Banja Luka and Prijedor CSBs -- did it take place? Did it happen?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The meeting in Banja Luka was scheduled for the 14th, I believe, and it was to begin at 11.00, with the leadership of the crime police in Banja Luka. Upon arrival in Banja Luka, we went to the centre, and that's when I first met the head of the crime police. I think it was Dusan Tegeltija at the time. He received me and my co-workers in his office. I supposed he was aware of our arrival and of the nature of the meeting. Since it was already past 11.00, I asked him whether he knew about the meeting, and he replied in the negative. After that, I went to the upper floor to see Mr. Zupljanin, chief of the Banja Luka CSB. I asked him whether he knew about the meeting. He invited me to a cup of coffee, but I met him on his way out. He was going to a meeting. And he said something like he was sorry. Actually, he said that he had forgotten to relate the information to the head of the crime enforcement service. The meeting had been scheduled by a dispatch that was sent. This generated a negative attitude toward Mr. Zupljanin on my part. Later, I found out that -- that the deputy chief, Djuro Bulic, was actually in charge of communication with the head of the crime enforcement service. This -- the latter, however - I mean Mr. Bulic - was absent at the time for private reasons. However, after that, there were no more communication problems with Mr. Bulic. Unfortunately, the meeting never took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It seems that part of your answer has not been recorded. Did you subsequently check the information that the failure to organise the meeting was due to Mr. Bulic's mistake? If so, who was the source of that information?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did check how -- how this came about. Mr. Bulic was absent for family reasons. He went to Belgrade and stayed there maybe even a month after the meeting. When I returned to the ministry, I couldn't but check why it had happened that way. And then I found out that it was up to him to organise the meeting and attend it. Generally speaking, Mr. Bulic was a responsible civil servant, and he proved that by his later work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise once more, but you are really going fast.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When Mr. Bulic was returning from Belgrade, did he come to the minister headquarters in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was actually on his way to Belgrade when he called at our headquarters. And then I asked him directly why it happened that way, because I wondered if there was -- there was some hidden reasons. And then he said that it was his personal mistake, not to acquaint the head of the crime enforcement service with the need to attend the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what happened after that? Where did you go after the meeting did not place at the Banja Luka CSB?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that we spent the night at the Bosna hotel. I believe it was the only place where one could find accommodation. And then we travelled on to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived at Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 8.30 and 9.00, we had already visited the SJB. That's when I first met Mr. Drljaca and his co-workers. He received us in a large meeting room. As far as I remember, apart from him, there was his assistant, the chief of the crime enforcement service, and the heads of the other services. I think that Prijedor had one or two police stations. Once they introduced themselves, we also introduced ourselves. I introduced myself as co-ordinator from the crime police administration and acting chief. I introduced my colleagues. And I stated the reason of our visit. I asked him whether he was familiar with the MUP dispatch and the dispatch from the centre. His reply was strange and surprising to us at the time. It was something like, I'm not interested about any dispatches, especially those from the CSB. My bosses never told me about the reason for this meeting. And then he said that, as far as he was concerned, the meeting was over and that we were free to go and have breakfast. After that, he and his colleagues stood up and so did we. The entire process took no longer than 15 or 20 minutes. As far as I remember, we went to a building. I think it was called Aviator's Club or something. We ordered coffee. And in the conversation with the man, I asked him, Do you know what you're doing? Do you know that this is an offence? And, after all, we've travelled a couple of hundred kilometres under difficult conditions. And then he replied in the same vain, My bosses never told me anything about this. And I'm almost fully certain that he told me that the bosses from the Crisis Staff, or, actually, the municipal authorities were the ones. I explained to him that I would report about it to my superiors. I refused to stay for breakfast, and just like he had said that the meeting was over, I replied -- I then said to him, for us, the breakfast was over. And we left for Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you inform anybody, and, if so, who, about this incident in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I informed Mr. Kovac, who was head of the public security department, or maybe acting head, as my -- because he was my immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are we talking about Mr. Tomo Kovac or another Kovac?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that his official name was Tomislav Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember Mr. Kovac's reaction? Did he say what he would do about it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we commented the situation in Prijedor. I was sorry that I possibly misinformed him that, due to Mr. Zupljanin's mistake, the meeting in Banja Luka was not held. Clearly he had to inform his superiors, but I don't remember because Mr. Zupljanin -- Mr. Stanisic, as minister, was actually on his way out already due to the pressures exerted on him. And through the Ministry of the Interior, the government had to be informed because this was a clear case of disobedience of an organisational unit to the leadership of that same organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Kovac informed the government about this situation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be certain. But, at any rate, he should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know what the situation at the Bosanski Samac SJB was?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the report drawn up after visiting the Doboj centre, and that covers the Samac SJB too, which was initially conducted by a mixed team and, later, by a team of crime police officers, information was collected to the effect that the Samac SJB was not acting in accordance with the Law on Internal Affairs. In other words, they didn't obey the orders of the ministry. They were, more or less, being commanded by the Crisis Staff of Samac municipality. I also learned from the same reports that the SJB chief was not appointed to that position, in keeping with the Law on Internal Affairs. In other words, he was not confirmed in his position by the ministry after conducting checks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever meet Mr. Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I forgot to point that out. Chief Stevan Todorovic. Sometime late in 1992, I met Mr. Todorovic. An incident occurred involving certain military units of the VRS, and he was arrested by members of military bodies. Information was gathered by the Ministry of the Interior, and after that, it became clear that Mr. Todorovic could no longer remain in that position. Late in 1992, he came by the Ministry of the Interior, acting slightly strange, looking slightly strange, and so on and so forth. As far as I was told, he was there to check his own status following those incidents and all the information that had been gathered about his work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who he was there to see?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was waiting with the secretary outside Mr. Kovac's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what he was told by Mr. Kovac about his status?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Kovac told him specifically, but I do remember a meeting at which a general conclusion was reached by Mr. Kovac and everybody else there that Mr. Todorovic had to be removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if he was eventually removed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not before the end of 1992, but he certainly was over the following months. Every time there was a removal that had to be done, the same thing transpired. In those municipalities where the local Crisis Staffs and the local leadership had significant influence over the work of the police stations, one had to carry out some political preparations, and there had to be political pressure by the leaders of the RS beforehand, in order to be able to make the appropriate replacements or removals, and in order for new people to be appointed to those positions. We had some negative experiences, when, for example, assessing that a certain person was not the right person for a certain position and then trying to remove that person, or, rather, the minister trying to remove that person from that position. Some local politicians and friends and acquaintances of those persons organised support rallies to voice their discontent at the fact that these persons were being removed from office. There was always the danger that the effect of the rallies might spill over to some military units of the VRS through the acquaintances, the supporters of this leader, or, indeed, the spokesperson himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you provide an example?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Textbook example would be the events at Pale municipality and the attempt that was made there to remove the public security station chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: His name?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Malko Koroman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When did that occur, the removal of the Pale public security station chief, Malko Koroman?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first half of 1992, but I can't remember the month. I know it was a large-scale incident with people gathering around the SJB building. Later on, I spoke to some friends who were members of the armed forces, and I heard that this was about to spill over also to some units of the VRS. This was an attempt to get them involved in the rallies too, in order to keep the person in office and make his removal impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was Malko Koroman eventually removed from that position; and, if so, when?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was early 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What about Simo Drljaca, as chief of the SJB? Was he, too, removed from that position; and, if so, when?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was early 1993. I think the minister at the time was Ratko Adzic at the time of Drljaca's removal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the initiatives for these three SJB chief removals - I'm talking about Malko Koroman, Stevan Todorovic, and Simo Drljaca - do you know when these initiatives were first launched?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about Mr. Todorovic. Chief of the CSB, Andrija Bjelosevic at the time, on several occasions, informed the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let's try and cut this short, if we can, sir. I want to know the year. When, if you know, the initiatives to remove these people from office occurred?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, 1D571, tab 69, is our next document. This is a report following inspection of the Foca, Cajnice, Rudo, and Visegrad SJBs. The date is the 14th of September, 1992. Signed by three names, Nikola Milanovic, Milomir Orasanin, Ostoja Minic. The three names are there, yet a single signature. Sir, are you familiar with this report?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What about the three persons whose names we can see at the bottom of the document? Which administration did these three persons belong to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crime police administration, of which I was then head.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was this an instructive visit; and was it pursuant to your orders that they went there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was such a visit. And it was pursuant to my order that these people were sent to the SJBs specified in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A while ago -- a while ago, you touched upon the question of the Trebinje CSB. What about Foca, Cajnice, Rudo and Visegrad? What about these SJBs? Which CSB did these belong to, in territorial terms?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: These SJBs, in territorial terms, belonged to the Trebinje CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: According to your information, did the Trebinje CSB encounter any difficulties, in relation to these four SJBs?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier on in my evidence, the problem had to do with all types of communications, and I mean roads and equipment. The representatives of the Trebinje CSB did not have a chance to tour these stations in order to see how well they were performing their tasks, or, indeed, in order to have a chance to see what sort of problems they were facing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was that the reason these inspectors were dispatched on an instructive tour? One of the reasons for that.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was one of the reasons they were dispatched.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 42D1, tab 84.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is a report bearing the date of the 29th of October, 1992. Addressed to the assistant minister for police and the assistant minister for crime prevention. Submitted by Inspector Ostoja Minic and Inspector Goran Saric. This is about taking into custody Milorad Tesic and Milan Kanlic in Brcko. Inspector and commander of the MUP being taken into custody by members of the military. Were you familiar with this case, sir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. In 1992, there were frequent incidents involving members of the VRS. There were individual and group attacks being carried out on members of the Ministry of the Interior. We used this kind of information to put together collective reports to cover all of our incidents involving the VRS. These were then to be submitted to the minister so he could get in touch with the leaders of the VRS to see if we could overcome these problems. Attacks were frequent. Men were often detained or taken into custody by individuals or groups from the military police or the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was this report meant for the RS government?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was meant for the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was your expectation that the government would take measures to deal with situations like these?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only natural to expect that the prime minister would take this up with his defence minister. The interior minister would be summoned too, and then they would get in touch with the leaders of the VRS to revolve these situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What about these inspectors who submitted the reports, Minic and Saric? Which ministry administration did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ostoja Minic belonged to the crime police administration, my own; and Mr. Goran Saric, to the police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless there are any objections, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- perhaps my learned friend could ask the witness if he received this document. He is one of the addressees. If he could just confirm that he received it in 1992, I might not have an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I thought it was apparent from his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, Mr. Macar, did you receive this report in the course of 1992, as is stated in the heading?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As can you see in the heading, although this is an mistake here, it says assistant minister for crime prevention, the inspector who carried out these checks, upon his return, typically informs his superior and then jointly they draw up the report, which is what you see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Have you had occasion to see this particular report?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Even, if I may be allowed to add, Mr. Minic and Saric drew up this report together in the premises of the crime police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I still didn't hear the answer, but I assume he means he did see it in 1992. And if that's the case, I don't have an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat my question again. You see now why it is important to give very concrete answers to questions so as not to waste time. We've lost five minutes over this. Did you receive this document back in 1992? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already said, I saw this document, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D643, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 118D1, tab 90.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is a report on the situation at the Gacko police station on 9 December 1992. Inspection was conducted and the situation assessed, following which we see that some measures were being proposed, and this document is signed by Milorad Cuk, chief of police. Do you know this Mr. Cuk; and can you tell us where he worked?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew Mr. Cuk. He was chief of police in the Trebinje CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Gacko police station fall under the Trebinje CSB?

utterances.speaker: GORAN MACAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Gacko police station belonged to the Trebinje CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, I'm going to show you P988, which is tab 104. This is the aide-memoire for instructive audit or inspection. We don't see the date.
